spiritual_reading.full_translation:
From zeal for what is right, the Divine brings whatever resists into the presence of truth, and that resistance at once loses its strength and is compelled into order under a just assessment.

The zeal you are permitted to have is not the delight of harming, but a righteous discernment that works for amendment. Toward those who are hard to lead, it presses for a change of mind. Its severity is chiefly a warning and a restraint, because it is not aimed at ruin but at turning back evil. The severity itself is the warning; and when the need is present, you may correct a companion with words that awaken fear, bringing him into a useful shame, so that stubborn resistance in his will may be removed and his interior intention may yield to what is right.

Yet there is another zeal that must be refused. It is the zeal that gives evil desire an opening and joins it with sin. It listens only to what flatters self, then burns from pride and self-display, fixing its attention on another in order to dominate. It does not speak what builds; instead it rages from arrogance and speaks from contempt. It defames to make the other seem worthless, refuses to acknowledge good, pours out abuse and condemnation, and longs to cast down what is gentle, repaying injury with injury and making retaliation its law. From this it either stirs others into wrongdoing, or, if someone falters, it seizes that fall as material for further condemnation and rejects any just evaluation. It withdraws into self-rule against the common understanding of companions; and when corrected, it converts that correction into a cause for rage and then commits evil from that rage. This is evil zeal, though it still takes the name of zeal.

A distinction must therefore be held between destructive rage and healing severity. When you must confront evil or stubborn falsity and someone hardens against instruction, you may see that he sinks into obstinacy and, from his own disorder, attributes harshness to you and returns harshness. Then what is required is not cruelty but firm, weighty truth that restrains and compels reflection. This should not be called rage, even if it is felt as painful; its true name is strong correction that aims at repentance.

The one who corrects rightly acts from understanding like a skillful healer whose perception is delicate and exact. The disorders to be removed may be severe, so the means are varied according to state. Sometimes what is needed is an ardent, searching truth that stings in order to cleanse; sometimes it is a gentle, soothing truth that binds and restores; and this is chosen according to the condition and according to what has preceded.

Thus there are some who accept sharp correction and are set right by it; and there are others who are harmed by sharpness and are restored only by humbling gentleness. The wise therefore adapts admonition to the state of the one being corrected, bringing down pride by truths fitted to its error until humility can acknowledge what is right. He also guards that his correction proceeds from what is godly within him so that his intention remains pure. He regards a companion in two modes: one by which he leads through love, and another by which he restrains through fear. For when stubborn resistance springs from foolish confidence and the delight of doing evil, fear can arrest it and so open a way to repentance. Yet even then the corrector remains ordered within himself, weighing words and their effect, and he persists until amendment is reached.

For the enlighteners in the higher heavens are manifested in these same two modes—love and fear—because their interior life flows through their whole being and presents itself fully. In the manifestation of love there is perceived beauty and elevation; in the manifestation of opposing presence there is perceived confrontation and restraint. By these two modes they cleanse and set in order the higher powers within those who receive their influence.

paragraph_translations.connection: OPENS the chapter’s action by introducing zeal as just ordering.

spiritual_reading.overall_coherence: Strong coherence: a single moral-spiritual argument progresses from just zeal, to the prohibition of prideful rage, to a discriminating method of correction, and finally to its archetype in heavenly manifestation. The main stumbles come from the source text’s broken syntax and duplications in ¶5 and ¶8, but the underlying twofold structure (love/fear; gentle/ardent correction) remains consistent throughout.

findings.diagnosis: Clean correspondential opening: a functional moral process (zeal → appearance before judgement → immediate withering/subduing) that the spiritual reading can narrate without forcing.
findings.evidence: Text moves by inner effect and outcome, not by ranks/jurisdictions: “Through anger… I will make him stand… shall wither and be subdued… come to the place of judgement with righteous judgement.” The spiritual reading did not stumble here and correctly treated it as an action-logic (“brings whatever resists into the presence of truth… compelled into order”).

findings.diagnosis: Genuine difficulty from physical-text damage (broken syntax, displaced clauses), not a foreign administrative insertion. The paragraph remains a single functional teaching about corrective severity; the reader’s stumble is due to scrambled segment order and lacunae around the ‘strip him of obduracy…heart’ line.
findings.evidence: The whole unit stays inside the same functional moral economy: anger-as-rebuke “is only a scare and a rebuke… not to destroy them… words that scare… shaming him to good use… strip him of the obduracy… his heart.” The spiritual reading explicitly notes forced reconstruction: “syntactically broken… ‘strip him of the obduracy…his heart’ forced a best-effort reading.” There is no shift to named powers, stations, authorities, or inventory lists—so the stumble is best explained by corruption/dislocation, not layering.

findings.diagnosis: Genuine difficulty from duplication/scrambling (likely dittography and/or conflation of two parallel formulations of ‘evil anger’), not an administrative overlay. The paragraph’s teaching remains consistent (prideful rage masquerading as zeal), but several short imperatival/observational clauses appear out of order and repeated, producing the reader’s ‘scrambled’ note.
findings.evidence: The narrative logic is coherent (evil desire → pride → domination → abusive speech → retaliation → refusal of judgement), but the surface text shows seams: “listen to him… look at him” + bracketed alternates (“[Do not]… [And if he does not]… [what pleases him,]”) and clausal pileup (“he is angry… and he is violent… he does not utter… composed anger; he is angry…”). The spiritual reading flags this directly: “Several clauses appear duplicated or scrambled (‘listen to him…look at him’).” No administrative markers (no lists of rulers, watches, powers) appear; the disruption is internal corruption of the same moral discourse.

findings.diagnosis: Mostly clean correspondential distinction (healing reprimand vs anger). One micro-stumble (“two or one matters”) is best explained as damaged/obscure idiom or a small displacement, not an insertion: the paragraph continues the functional diagnosis of states and their proper remedy.
findings.evidence: Core line is clear and non-administrative: “they will not be able to name it anger; rather its name is the strong reprimand that leads to repentance.” The reader’s only uncertainty is localized: “‘Two or one matters’ was unclear.” Removing that phrase would not change voice or improve narrative in a meaningful way; it reads like a fragmentary connective inside the same teaching, not a foreign block.

findings.diagnosis: Clean substrate teaching with heavy local corruption in ¶8 (fragmentation, intrusive bracketed doublets), producing forced ‘stitching’ by the spiritual reader. The underlying correspondential structure (doctor/remedies → hot/cool → love/fear) is stable; the problem is textual damage and conflation, not administrative layering.
findings.evidence: ¶7 is a tight functional simile: “wise doctor… wounds… sometimes… remedy that is hot… sometimes… remedy that is cool… according to the state.” ¶8 preserves the same functional method but is visibly broken by repeated starters and bracketed alternates: “Through the hard word [is like] the blow… [So also there are two kinds]… [while another kind]… [and be harmed,]” plus disrupted logic around “the brother in two aspects… love… fear… obduracy… foolishness.” The spiritual reading admits reconstruction: “paragraph is heavily fragmented… required stitching… without preserving the broken natural syntax.” The consistent method (adaptation by state; love/fear as modes) argues against insertion; an insertion would more likely introduce jurisdictions/named powers rather than re-state the same functional analogy in damaged form.

findings.diagnosis: Clean correspondential cosmic grounding: ‘light-givers’ manifested in love/fear as modes that purify. This is not administrative (no chain of command); it universalizes the same functional two-aspect method established earlier. The reader did not stumble here.
findings.evidence: Text stays in mode-of-operation language: “revealed with these two aspects… love… fear… appearances… beauty and sublimity… confrontation… they shall purify… powers above.” The spiritual reading smoothly extends the argument (“archetype in heavenly manifestation”) and reports no mismatch of voice or narrative break.

textual_criticism.summary: No administrative overlay or seam-expansion is diagnostically present in this chapter. All stumbles reported by the spiritual reading (¶4, ¶5, ¶8; minor in ¶6) are best explained as damaged transmission: scrambled clause order, dittography/doublets, and fragmentation within an otherwise coherent correspondential (functional) teaching. Recommendations: 0 excisions, 0 annotations, 7 none (with 3–4 noted as ‘genuine difficulty’ due to corruption rather than layering).
